text:
Toronto’s leading candidates to be mayor talk to the Star’s editorial board about the most difficult matters facing the city and their campaigns.
 Brad Bradford and Olivia Chow are the leading candidates in Toronto’s mayoralty race.
 R.J. Johnston photos/Toronto Star
 With their electoral showdown less than two weeks away, the leading contenders to be mayor of Toronto offered acutely different visions of the city’s present and its future Wednesday.
 Incumbent Olivia Chow and councillor Brad Bradford each spent an hour fielding questions from Star journalists on some of the most pressing issues facing Torontonians in separate meetings with this newspaper’s editorial board.
 The candidates gave in-depth answers about their plans for the city budget, their leadership styles, and how they would address the interwoven problems of homelessness, addiction and public safety.
 Here are some of the at-times thorny issues they took on.
 Bradford offers new details of how he’d find the money
 Bradford, the councillor for Beaches—East York, has grabbed headlines during the campaign with big-ticket promises. On Wednesday, he said his campaign is based on “fiscal discipline,” and offered additional details about how he would pay for his ideas.
 He provided a handout to Star journalists, indicating his pledge to hire 1,000 new police officers would be funded through the “annual budget review process.” (This would be separate from the line-by-line review he’s proposed.)
 Why Olivia Chow and Brad Bradford supporters see Toronto as ‘two different cities’
 Bradford’s team predicts the police hiring plan would cost an estimated $143 million when fully implemented in its fourth year. The councillor said it’s not unreasonable to expect to find enough savings in the city’s existing budget to help pay for the new officers.
 “We’re going to find savings at city hall,” he said.
 Bradford predicted his plan to provide refunds to TTC passengers for delays of 15 minutes — pegged at $3.5 million to $7 million annually — could be “absorbed” into the existing TTC budget by improving the reliability of the transit system and attracting more paying riders. (TTC officials have projected the cost of a refund program would be higher than Bradford’s estimate and as much as upwards of $50 million. Currently, the agency is projecting a $148 million shortfall for 2027.) 
 A more expensive transit policy — installing platform edge doors at subway stations — would be funded, said Bradford, through his plan to eliminate the annual practice of using hundreds of millions of dollars from the operating budget to pay for infrastructure. He said it’s a measure that could also free up money for other policy proposals.
 Bradford has also promised to freeze the residential property tax rate in his first year (he has said he would maintain the annual council-approved 1.5 per cent hike for the city building fund), while protecting front-line services. But he didn’t rule out raising taxes or taking on more debt later in his term to pay for his priorities.
 “I think you would assess it based on the context of the situation and the time,” he said when asked if those options were on the table.
 In her editorial board meeting, Chow said Bradford’s plan amounted to making promises and saying “I can find the money somewhere.” She charged that his policies are so expensive he couldn’t deliver them without cutting services. “I’m doing the math. Someone contradict my math,” she said.
 Bradford denies disparaging colleagues 
 Bradford rejected an allegation in a recent story in news outlet The Local that, according to unnamed former staffers, he referred to women councillors using the word “bitch.”
 “Absolutely not true,” he said.
 Asked about reports that he can be difficult to work with, Bradford described himself as a “passionate guy” who is trying to do his best for the city, and said he could co-operate with councillors he disagreed with if elected.
 “I’m pretty relentless in the pursuit of things that need to be fixed, and you know I want to work with everybody to get that done,” he said.
 Chow defends handling of fallout from Gaza war and security concerns of Jewish community
 Chow has faced intense scrutiny from some quarters for her handling of the local reverberations of the war in Gaza. She has also received criticism that she’s been insufficiently empathetic to fears from Toronto’s Jewish community at a time of rising hate crimes.
 She said the “only thing” she hasn’t done was attend the Walk for Israel, “because I do not agree with what the Israeli government is doing and I’ve said so,” said Chow, who has called Israel’s attack on Gaza after the Oct. 7 massacre perpetrated by Hamas a genocide.
 “I do as much as I can in supporting the Jewish community in Toronto. But I will not shy away about criticizing what’s happening in Gaza, because I do not agree with it and I have a right to say so.”
 When asked why she supported the so-called “bubble zone” bylaw, which limits protests around specific institutions — a decision that angered pro-Palestine protesters — Chow said residents have a right to access child care centres and synagogues. The bylaw was created after a large protest at a Thornhill synagogue promoting illegal land sales in the occupied West Bank. The Star revealed last year that the city solicitor advised Toronto city council before the vote that the city would likely lose a court challenge as the bylaw could be unconstitutional.
 Chow denies she’s lacking ‘bold’ ideas
 Chow, who is seeking a second term, has mostly stuck to building on policies she’d drafted while in office during this campaign. 
 When asked where are the “bold ideas” from a progressive mayor, she insisted her proposals to expand her mid-morning snack program for all kids to lunch, freeze TTC fares and implement a weekly cap are ambitious.
 She argued there’s no point in making big promises that are not realistic. “Where are we now with SmartTrack?” Chow said, referencing John Tory’s 2014 campaign promise of a 22-stop regional line that has shrunk to just three stations and has blown over budget.
 Chow and Bradford divided on involuntary treatment for addiction
 Chow was asked by a member of the editorial board what he should tell his daughter the city is doing to care for the people in crisis she sees on her way to school.
 Chow answered that he should take her to Dunn House, a supportive housing site for homeless Torontonians that opened in 2024. She recounted the story of Jason Miles, one of the home’s residents who lived on the streets for years but has “become a gardener and a role model.”
 “His life had been transformed because of housing. You cannot heal, you cannot turn your life around, unless there’s a roof over your head,” she said.
 The city is now working on a much larger Dunn House-style building, to be completed in 2028. 
 Bradford recently joined a chorus of municipal leaders across Canada advocating for a controversial involuntary addiction treatment policy, an approach Chow rejects. 
 Asked whether the lack of evidence to support the efficacy of involuntary treatment gives him pause, the councillor insisted that “what we’re doing right now is not working,” and “it’s not a compassionate response from the city of Toronto to allow these people to languish on the streets and in the parks and on the transit system.”

When does a school’s failure to respond to bullying become a legal liability?

A recent California appellate court ruling offers an important warning for school leaders.
In E.I. v. El Segundo Unified School District, a student who experienced ongoing bullying was awarded $1 million in damages. The court found that while some disciplinary decisions may be discretionary, failing to follow a district’s own bullying-response policies can be an operational failure — and schools can be held accountable.

Documentation alone isn't enough. If bullying continues after it has been reported, schools need to demonstrate that they took consistent, ongoing steps to address it.
This isn't simply about avoiding a lawsuit. It's about creating a school environment where students feel safe, supported, and ready to learn.

Read the full article by Dr. Melinda Bossenmeyer on the Peaceful Playgrounds website.

text:
In the only title bout ever held there in its' 56-year history, Joey Archibald (left) wins a 15-round majority decision over "The Bronx Spider", Mike Belloise, to capture the vacant NYSAC World Featherweight Championship on October 17, 1938 at the St. Nicholas Arena in New York City.

Archibald had previously beaten Belloise on July 11, 1938, on points in a close ten-round unanimous decision in Washington, D.C. Joey Archibald was managed by Al Weill, and his trainer was Charlie Goldman. 

Archibald and Belloise, the brother of 1940s Middleweight contender and two time World Title challenger Steve Belloise, were chosen to fight for the title by commissioners of the New York State Athletic Commission, causing some controversy as several top contenders were overlooked. The National Boxing Association had previously decided to give recognition to Archibald if he could subsequently defeat Leo Rodak.

Belloise started strong in the first before a vocal crowd of nearly 7,000, but dropped the second through the fifth rounds to Archibald's continuous blows to his waist and body. In the sixth, Belloise was staggered by Archibald with a succession of hooks that drove him across the ring. In the eleventh through the fifteenth, Archibald came back to gain dominance. Two of the three judges gave the bout to Archibald, with the referee scoring it a draw, while Ed Hughes of the Brooklyn Daily Eagle unofficially gave ten rounds to Archibald, three to Belloise, and two even. In similar scoring, the United Press gave nine rounds to Archibald, with three to Belloise, and three even.

On December 5, 1938, while still holding the NYSAC featherweight title, Archibald lost to Petey Scalzo in a second-round knockout at Royal Windsor Arena in New York. The bout was not a title fight, and certainly not recognized as one by the National Boxing Association (NBA), a sanctioning body with a wider range and more prestige than the NYSAC. In the first round, Archibald received a hard right to the chin, but managed to rally to keep the round even. After finding an opening in the second round, Scalzo delivered three powerful right hooks to the chin of Archibald that dropped him 2 minutes, and 10 seconds after the bell. The win would cement Scalzo as the leading contender for the National Boxing Association's world featherweight championship, though Archibald's management never scheduled a rematch.

Archibald would gain universal recognition, and the NBA world Featherweight Championship, when he defeated Leo Rodak on April 18, 1939, in a fifteen-round points decision at Rhode Island Auditorium in Providence. Rodak was considered the top contender for the NYSAC world featherweight title. Archibald was the aggressor throughout his bout with Rodak, and landed the most punches in the opinion of the referee who scored for him. The Associated Press gave seven rounds to Archibald, with six for Rodak and two even. Both fighters committed fouls in the eleventh, a round declared even by the referee as was the closely fought seventh. In the thirteenth and fourteenth, with the bout close but Archibald leading by a shade, Rodak broke loose and gained the advantage with long and wary rights. The fifteenth clearly went to Archibald. After the fight, Rodak's manager complained of frequent low blows by Archibald.

Archibald would hold neither title very long.

He defeated Henry Jeffra in his first defense of the Featherweight World Championship on a 15-round split decision on September 28th of 1939, at Griffith Stadium in Washington, D.C. The referee was the legendary ex-lightweight champion Benny Leonard, who scored ten rounds for Archibald, with only four for Jeffra, though one judged seriously dissented giving ten rounds to Jeffra. The remaining judge gave nine rounds to Archibald. The sports writers who covered the bout unanimously favored Jeffra, as did the crowd of 10,000 who heavily booed and threw newspapers into the ring for five minutes after the split decision was announced.

The NBA (National Boxing Association, which eventually became the WBA) withdrew its recognition of Archibald in April of 1940 for his refusal to fight several of the leading contenders, particularly Petey Scalzo.

Archibald would lose the NYSAC (and Baltimore) version of the World Featherweight Championship to Harry Jeffra on May 20, 1940, via 15-round unanimous decision at the Coliseum in Baltimore. 

Archibald would regain the NYSAC version of the title from Jeffra on May 12th of 1941, in a fifteen-round split decision at Griffith Stadium in Washington but, once again, lose it very quickly.

His next challenger, on September 11th of 1941, Chalky Wright, dropped Archibald to the canvas 54 seconds into the eleventh with a left hook and a powerful straight right, Wright was well ahead on points before the knockout, as Archibald had lost the first eight rounds by a substantial margin. 

Joseph John Archibald, who'd attended Providence College and studied for the priesthood in his youth, would lose an 8-round points decision to Willie Pep in his next bout giving a good effort in a one-sided loss and his skills were clearly in decline; he'd lose 27 of his remaining 34 bouts to finish his career at 60-42-5 with 29 KO wins.

Joey Archibald died in 1998 at the age of 83.
--------------------------------------------------------
From The New Jersey Boxing Hall of Fame website on "The Bronx Spider" Mike Belloise:

A few months ago, Steve Belloise Jr. sent us an article on his dad. Now, here is Steve’s cousin, also named Steve, who writes on his dad, the great Mike Belloise.
“He was a craftsman in the ring.” That’s what my teacher said. “They couldn’t lay a glove on him,” a business associate once informed me. “He spent hours in the gym when I was a kid and taught me everything he knew, we fought towards the end of his career and when I beat him we both cried in the middle of the ring,” ex-fighter Chester Rico reminisced.
Whether it was memories of a passionate fan or testimony from a worthy competitor, I grew up hearing nothing but the sincerest praise for Mike Belloise, my father. The first of nine children born to Salvatore and Julia Belloisi in the Villa Avenue section of the Bronx, Mike began a long, difficult road to stardom in the mid-1920s.
All told, he fought over 200 amateur fights, including pre-Olympic tours in 1928 and 1931 for the U.S. Boxing Team during which Belloise took home medals from all over Europe. In 1932, Mike had paid his dues and was ready to begin a pro career.
Fighting as often as three times a month, Mike roared through his first 22 matches undefeated until he was decisioned by Lew Feldman in January 1934. In June of that same year, Belloise avenged the loss, turning the tables on Feldman, winning a 10-round decision on his way to an elimination bout the following month with Baby Arizmendi for the vacated World Featherweight Title. 
In a grueling struggle, Mike lost a 15-round decision and his title chances were temporarily shelved. 
By all accounts, Belloise had “style.” Though he was not a knockout artist, he was known as a crisp puncher who never offered an opponent a clear shot. To confuse his adversaries, Mike, a natural righty, would sometimes switch to southpaw stance in the middle of a fight. 
His ability to tag opponents with a variety of punches without providing them the opportunity to land counter blows earned him the nickname, “The Bronx Spider.”
It took nearly two years, but by 1936, with a record of 35-4-3, Mike had earned another title shot. Belloise was determined to not let this chance get away and fulfilled a lifelong dream by knocking out Everett Rightmire in the 14th round to become Featherweight Champion of the World.
In that same year, Belloise fought perhaps his greatest bout which, ironically, was a loss. Mike went ten rounds with the immortal Henry Armstrong and even knocked down the ring legend. However, Armstrong escaped with a split decision.
Years later, Belloise, whose charismatic personality had made him a crowd favorite even in distant California, gave an account to The New York Post of the tumultuous scene that ensued after this unpopular decision. “Of course I wasn’t happy with the outcome, but what I remember seeing is Mae West at ringside giving the referee hell and I coudn’t help but get a kick out of it.”
In June of 1937, at his fighting peak, Belloise suddenly contracted an illness which thrust him into a life and death struggle and resulted in the removal of one of his ribs. Though he was able to return the following year, Mike eventually lost his title, dropping a 15-round decision to Joey Archibald in October 1938. However, this was no time for self pity, because another Belloise was about to make his mark on the boxing world.
At about this time, Mike began getting fights on his undercards for his brother Steve. Though Mike recognized that his brother was younger and relatively inexperienced, he believed that Steve could make up for his lack of ring experience with punching power. As it turned out, Steve became a wonderful boxer as well as a terrifying puncher, winning 95 out of 110 fights, 59 by knockout. 
Art Rust Jr., renowned boxing analyst, put it like this: “Steve had a big edge being Mike’s younger brother and getting on his fight cards. He never even fought an amateur fight, but he didn’t have to, he was that good!” 
As for Mike, he continued to fight the best fighters of his time, including the likes of AI Reid, Petey Scalzo and Lew Jenkins. After losing the aforementioned bout in 1942 with his old friend Chester Rico, Mike announced his retirement. But boxing was in his blood and he could not stay away. He came back later that year to rip off four consecutive wins and stayed around until 1947, when he hung up the gloves for good at age 36.
When Mike passed away in 1969 at the much too early age of 58, he left behind a legacy of guile, character and courage. He was idolized by those who watched from afar, worshipped by his peers and loved by the ones who knew him best.
What I wouldn’t do to go back and spend just one Friday night in the late-1930s, ringside at the Bronx Arena, watching Steve Belloise take apart his foe with savage right hand counters on his way to stardom, then witness as Mike Belloise, still ring wise, still master of the square circle, land countless jabs and slip punches, frustrating yet another opponent into hopeless resignation. Sadly, none of us will ever see a night like that again, except perhaps in the mind’s eye of an old-time boxing aficianado who still remembers the Belloise brothers and their place in boxing lore.

text:
Holding Southern California Edison Accountable: Fighting for Reliable Power in Ventura County

By: Jeff Gorell, Chair of the Ventura County Board of Supervisors

Ventura County residents should not have to choose between wildfire safety and reliable electricity. Southern California Edison’s (SCE) Public Safety Power Shutoffs (PSPS) have left families, businesses, and entire communities facing prolonged outages, often with little certainty about when power will be restored.

While preventing wildfires must remain a top priority, the frequency, duration, and disruption of these shutoffs demand greater accountability. That is why I have made it a priority to challenge SCE, secure meaningful improvements, and advocate for long-term solutions that better protect our communities.

Public Safety Power Shutoffs emerged in response to devastating wildfires and substantial lawsuits against electric utilities. California’s regulatory framework allows utilities to proactively de-energize power lines during dangerous weather conditions to reduce wildfire ignition risks. While these shutoffs can prevent catastrophic fires, their widespread use has created serious challenges for our communities.

One common misconception is that under grounding power lines eliminates the possibility of shutoffs. Under grounding offers significant benefits for reliability, wildfire risk reduction, and neighborhood aesthetics, but it does not guarantee uninterrupted electricity. Underground lines may still depend on aboveground or sensitive infrastructure elsewhere in the local circuit, and therefore the entire circuit would be subject to PSPS, even neighborhoods with underground power.

Following widespread outages in January 2025, I directly engaged SCE leadership to demand improvements in restoration times, communication, and coordination with local emergency officials. Our advocacy has produced meaningful concessions from Edison. SCE agreed to assign an employee to Ventura County’s Operational Area Emergency Operations Center during emergencies, improving direct communication and coordination with local public safety agencies. The utility has also improved its public communications and outage mapping tools, helping residents better understand which communities may be affected. They have also brought in a very forward leaning local representative, Ian Anderson, who has been engaged and responsive to residents.  

Importantly, Edison has committed to faster re-energization following shutoffs, recognizing the tremendous hardship extended outages create for residents and businesses.These improvements did not happen on their own. They resulted from persistent engagement, direct conversations, and our insistence that Ventura County residents deserve better.

text:
APPLE TO VETERANS: THANK YOU FOR YOUR SERVICE. NOW GET TO THE BACK OF THE LINE.

Apple 

Apple offers a generous 10% discount to active-duty military personnel and veterans through its separate online Military Store. And while we appreciate that discount, apparently it comes with a catch: We don’t get the same opportunity to purchase newly released products as customers paying full price.

Let me explain what happened with this morning’s iPhone Duo launch.

Customers shopping through Apple’s regular website were given the opportunity to prepare their orders in advance. They could select their phone, configure it, enter their payment information, and have everything ready to go. When preorders opened this morning, all they had to do was click Buy.

Military customers? Not so much.

We weren’t given that same advance preparation option. We couldn’t even save our configured orders.

Instead, we had to wait until the Military Store opened, go through id me to verify our military eligibility, return to Apple’s Military Store, configure our phones from scratch, enter our payment information, and THEN attempt to place our orders.

And to add insult to injury, the Military Store didn’t even open at the same time as the regular store. It was approximately seven minutes late.

Seven minutes might sound insignificant. But anyone familiar with an Apple product launch knows that those first few minutes can mean the difference between receiving your phone on launch day and waiting weeks or even months.

By the time military customers could get through the process, delivery estimates had already slipped from the October 23 launch date into mid-November.

So, in practice, Apple presented veterans with a choice:

Pay full price and have the same opportunity as everyone else to secure an early delivery.

Or accept your military discount, start behind everyone else, and hope there’s something left by the time you finish jumping through Apple’s hoops.

Let me be perfectly clear: We are not asking to be placed ahead of regular customers. We’re asking not to be placed BEHIND them simply because we’re using a benefit Apple proudly advertises.

What kind of appreciation is that?

Apple’s message to the military might as well be:

“Thank you for your service. Here’s 10% off. Now get to the back of the line so the people paying full price can order first.”

If Apple genuinely values the military community, why wasn’t its Military Store given the same preorder preparation tools and the same launch-time access as its regular store?

And don’t let them tell you this is a glitch. Do your own research on Reddit. This has been going on for years. Veterans don’t expect priority, but we do expect the same opportunity and not to be punished for taking advantage of for Apple’s military discount. ￼￼

A military discount should be a benefit, not a penalty.

Thanks, Apple, for the public display of appreciation. It’s a shame that when it actually matters, your treatment of military customers tells a different story.

Respect shouldn’t disappear at checkout.

Denver Harris
U.S. Navy Veteran

text:
THE DAY ROCK AND ROLL BECAME A RECORDING OF ITSELF

Billy Gibbons, ZZ Top, the price of a legendary career, and the slow disappearance of musical authenticity

I used to love ZZ Top.

And that is precisely why writing this is so damn painful.

Not because Billy Gibbons has grown old. Not because Dusty Hill is gone. Not because the extraordinary musical chemistry that once defined ZZ Top can never be fully recreated.

Those are the unavoidable consequences of time.

What troubles me is something entirely different.

The possibility that one of the greatest blues-rock guitarists in American history has become part of a musical spectacle in which the preservation of a profitable legend matters more than the living art that created it.

I recently watched a concert clip of ZZ Top that sparked an angry discussion among musicians and longtime fans.

One guitarist wrote that he would never pay to see such a performance. His complaint was simple. He could hear guitar parts while Billy Gibbons apparently wasn't playing them.

He wanted his live music live.

I understood his anger immediately.

Because I had experienced that same disappointment more than twenty years earlier.

On December 27, 2003, I realized that ZZ Top was using prerecorded backing tracks in concert.

I remember how it felt.

Not like discovering that a musician had missed a note or played a disappointing solo.

Something worse.

The uncomfortable realization that what I believed was a spontaneous musical experience was, at least partly, being reproduced mechanically.

And once that realization enters your mind, something changes.

You begin listening differently.

You begin watching the musicians' hands.

You begin wondering which sounds are being created onstage and which were created somewhere else.

And eventually you find yourself asking a question that should never become necessary at a rock concert.

What exactly am I paying to hear?

That question has followed me for nearly twenty-three years.

And today, with artificial intelligence rapidly transforming music production, it has become more important than ever.

BEFORE THE BEARDS, THERE WAS A GUITARIST

Before criticizing what ZZ Top has become, we need to remember what ZZ Top actually accomplished.

And those accomplishments were extraordinary.

Billy Gibbons was not manufactured by the music industry.

He emerged from the Texas blues and psychedelic rock scene as a genuinely gifted young guitarist.

With the Moving Sidewalks, he opened for Jimi Hendrix.

And Hendrix noticed him.

Think about the significance of that.

Jimi Hendrix was transforming the electric guitar into an instrument of possibilities nobody had previously imagined.

His playing expanded the vocabulary of rock music. His use of amplification, feedback, distortion, phrasing and physical expression changed the way generations of musicians approached the instrument.

And this extraordinary musician recognized something special in young Billy Gibbons.

Gibbons has recalled Hendrix praising his guitar playing, and the famous story of Hendrix naming him among America's finest young guitarists has become part of rock history.

The precise wording has been repeated in different forms over the years, but the admiration itself is an important part of Gibbons' story.

Billy didn't become famous because someone handed him a guitar and invented a personality around it.

He could play.

And he could play exceptionally well.

His great talent was never about playing the largest number of notes.

It was about knowing which notes mattered.

His phrasing was economical, his tone unmistakable, his timing extraordinary.

He understood something that separates great blues guitarists from technically impressive but musically forgettable players.

A single note, played with the right intention at the right moment, can communicate more than a hundred notes played without conviction.

Then came Dusty Hill and Frank Beard.

And one of the most remarkable power trios in American rock history was born.

THREE MUSICIANS AND AN ENTIRE MUSICAL UNIVERSE

Billy Gibbons, Dusty Hill and Frank Beard created a musical identity that was instantly recognizable.

There was nothing accidental about their success.

Gibbons supplied the guitar vocabulary, the unmistakable voice and much of the band's musical direction.

Dusty Hill brought a powerful rhythmic foundation, an outstanding musical partnership with Frank Beard and a personality that became inseparable from the group's identity.

And Frank Beard, despite being the only member without the famous beard, provided the disciplined, deceptively sophisticated drumming that made the entire machine work.

Together they understood groove.

Not simply keeping time.

Groove.

That almost mysterious interaction between rhythm, timing, anticipation and restraint that makes people move before they have consciously decided to move.

Listen to La Grange.

Listen to Tush.

Listen to Waiting for the Bus and Jesus Just Left Chicago.

Listen to Blue Jean Blues.

There is an entire musical education in those recordings.

And when ZZ Top embraced synthesizers, drum machines and new production techniques during the Eliminator era, they demonstrated that technology and artistic identity were not necessarily enemies.

Sharp Dressed Man and Gimme All Your Lovin' became enormous hits without completely erasing the musical personality that had made the band famous.

Their commercial success was extraordinary.

Their influence reached far beyond Texas.

ZZ Top opened for the Rolling Stones in Honolulu in 1972, an early milestone that placed the young band on the same bill as one of the biggest names in rock and roll.

Eventually, ZZ Top became one of the most successful and recognizable rock bands in the world.

And they deserved that success.

Their music was original in its personality, unmistakable in its sound and deeply connected to the American blues tradition.

But that last point brings me to another uncomfortable chapter in their history.

LA GRANGE AND THE JOHN LEE HOOKER QUESTION

For years, La Grange was one of the ZZ Top songs I admired most.

That hypnotic boogie rhythm.

The guitar tone.

The confidence.

The almost effortless way the song builds its momentum.

But the more I learned about the history of the blues, the more complicated my admiration became.

Because the foundation of La Grange bears an unmistakable relationship to the boogie tradition associated with John Lee Hooker, particularly his groundbreaking Boogie Chillen'.

And eventually that relationship became the subject of a federal copyright lawsuit.

The case was La Cienega Music Co. v. ZZ Top.

An important distinction is often lost when people retell the story.

John Lee Hooker did not personally file the lawsuit.

It was brought by La Cienega Music Company, associated with Bernard Besman, Hooker's former producer, which controlled publishing interests connected to Hooker's early recordings.

Hooker himself publicly distanced himself from the litigation.

The dispute concerned the musical relationship between La Grange and Boogie Chillen', not Hooker's song Boom Boom, as some retellings incorrectly suggest.

The court proceedings eventually produced a remarkable result.

ZZ Top prevailed.

But the legal reasoning deserves attention.

The dispute turned in significant part on the copyright treatment of older sound recordings under the Copyright Act of 1909.

The Ninth Circuit concluded that the distribution of the original Boogie Chillen' records had consequences for the copyright status of the underlying composition because of the law governing publication and copyright notice at the time.

The ruling exposed a serious problem in the protection of older musical works, particularly recordings from an era when many blues musicians lacked the resources, legal representation and business sophistication enjoyed by later generations of commercially successful artists.

Congress subsequently addressed the broader issue through legislation in 1997.

Now, I want to be careful here.

Winning a copyright lawsuit does not automatically establish artistic originality.

But losing one does not automatically establish deliberate theft either.

The blues developed through a long tradition of shared rhythms, musical phrases, borrowed structures, reinterpretation and personal transformation.

That history cannot be reduced to a simple accusation that one guitarist stole from another.

Nevertheless, the moral question remains.

What responsibility do commercially successful musicians have toward the artists and traditions from which their music emerged?

A court can determine what the law permits.

It cannot determine the full measure of artistic generosity, historical recognition or cultural responsibility.

And that is where my disappointment begins.

Not because ZZ Top was influenced by John Lee Hooker.

Influence is the bloodstream of music.

But because a legal victory built around the technicalities of an old copyright system can leave a bitter taste when the underlying musical tradition was created by artists who often received far less financial reward than the musicians who followed them.

John Lee Hooker helped establish a musical vocabulary that became enormously valuable to generations of rock musicians.

That contribution deserves more than a footnote.

It deserves acknowledgment, respect and a serious understanding of the economic history of American popular music.

For me, the La Grange controversy was an early reminder that commercial success and artistic integrity are not always the same thing.

And now, watching the argument over ZZ Top's live performances, I find myself confronting that distinction again.

WHEN A LIVE PERFORMANCE STOPS BEING LIVE

I have played music.

I know what it means to stand with other musicians and create something that exists only because those particular people are listening to one another at that particular moment.

There is an extraordinary difference between playing music and reproducing music.

That difference is not merely philosophical.

It has a foundation in human psychology and neuroscience.

During a live musical performance, musicians constantly anticipate one another's actions.

The drummer responds to the bass player.

The bass player responds to the guitarist.

The guitarist recognizes tiny changes in timing, dynamics and phrasing.

These interactions occur through continuous cycles of perception, prediction and correction.

Researchers studying interpersonal synchronization and joint musical performance have demonstrated that coordinated music-making involves complex interactions between attention, motor control, timing and social cognition.

And the audience participates in this process.

Not by playing instruments, but through perception, expectation and emotional engagement.

We recognize the tension of an uncertain musical moment.

We experience the release when the musicians find their way through it.

We hear the difference between a mechanical repetition and a phrase that emerges spontaneously from the interaction between human beings.

This does not mean that prerecorded music cannot move us emotionally.

Of course it can.

Some of the most powerful musical experiences of our lives come from recordings.

But a live concert offers something additional.

The knowledge that the performance is happening now.

That it involves physical effort, risk, judgment and real-time decisions.

That something unexpected might occur.

That a guitarist might miss a note, discover a better phrase or suddenly take the music somewhere nobody anticipated.

That uncertainty is not a defect.

It is part of the artistic value.

And when prerecorded material begins replacing the central musical actions that audiences believe they are witnessing, the relationship between performer and listener changes.

The sound may remain convincing.

The experience may remain entertaining.

But the authenticity of the event becomes questionable.

And that matters.

THE MILLI VANILLI QUESTION

I remember the Milli Vanilli scandal.

And I remember why people were furious.

The problem wasn't simply that the recordings sounded bad.

They didn't.

The problem was that audiences had been led to believe they were watching and supporting the actual singers whose voices appeared on the records.

The public presentation and the musical reality were fundamentally different.

And when that distinction became impossible to ignore, the entire enterprise collapsed.

Now, let me make something absolutely clear.

Billy Gibbons is not Milli Vanilli.

Comparing their musical achievements would be absurd.

Billy Gibbons is a historically important guitarist with decades of genuine artistic accomplishment.

But the ethical principle exposed by the Milli Vanilli scandal remains relevant.

Audiences deserve to understand what they are experiencing.

A prerecorded keyboard texture is one thing.

A supplementary sound effect is another.

But hearing substantial instrumental parts while the musician supposedly responsible for them is not actually performing raises a different question.

Especially when those parts are central to the artistic identity being sold.

I have no objection to technology assisting musicians.

I have no objection to additional musicians.

I have no objection to rearranging songs because age, physical limitations or personnel changes make the original arrangements difficult.

But why pretend that the original experience can be mechanically preserved forever?

If another guitarist is needed, hire another guitarist.

If a song needs a different arrangement, change the arrangement.

If the performance is going to depend substantially on prerecorded material, tell the audience.

There is nothing dishonorable about honesty.

The dishonor begins when the appearance of live musical accomplishment becomes more important than the accomplishment itself.

THE TRAGEDY OF AGING ROCK LEGENDS

This is where the subject becomes genuinely painful.

Because the musicians who created the great rock culture of the 1960s and 1970s are growing old.

Some are dealing with serious physical limitations.

Some have lost bandmates and lifelong collaborators.

Some can no longer reproduce the performances that made them famous.

And some continue touring because the commercial demand for their legendary names remains enormous.

I do not believe growing old diminishes an artist's dignity.

Quite the opposite.

Aging can bring depth, restraint, emotional intelligence and a musical perspective unavailable to younger performers.

A great guitarist does not need to play with the physical aggression of his twenties to produce extraordinary music in his eighties.

Sometimes a slower phrase contains more emotional meaning than a spectacular display of youthful technique.

But there is a distinction between adapting one's art to age and concealing the deterioration of a performance behind an increasingly elaborate technological production.

And that distinction deserves serious discussion.

The aging musician is not the enemy.

The aging body is not a moral failure.

The problem emerges when the machinery surrounding a legendary career becomes unwilling to acknowledge that time has changed the artistic possibilities.

Aging is a biological reality.

Pretending that nothing has changed is a commercial decision.

And when the commercial decision begins undermining the artistic experience, fans have every right to question it.

Especially fans who have spent decades supporting those musicians.

THE ARRIVAL OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE

Now we arrive at the larger question.

Artificial intelligence.

A technology I follow with enormous curiosity and genuine enthusiasm.

I believe AI may eventually transform our understanding of intelligence, creativity and perhaps consciousness itself.

I see extraordinary possibilities in its development.

But I also see a growing cultural danger.

We are becoming capable of generating increasingly sophisticated musical performances without the traditional human processes that once produced them.

AI systems can already create convincing songs, arrangements, instrumental textures and vocal performances.

And their capabilities will continue to improve.

That development is technologically remarkable.

But the cultural consequences depend upon how we choose to use it.

A computer-generated guitar solo may eventually become acoustically indistinguishable from a performance by a gifted human musician.

Yet the sound alone does not necessarily contain everything we value about musical performance.

When I watch a great guitarist play, I am not simply receiving an arrangement of frequencies.

I am witnessing a human being translating intention into physical action.

I am watching a lifetime of practice, experience, musical memory and emotional expression unfold in real time.

The musician's body is part of the instrument.

The hands matter.

The timing matters.

The hesitation matters.

The decision to play one note instead of another matters.

And the interaction with other musicians matters.

AI may reproduce the acoustic result.

But reproducing the result is not necessarily equivalent to reproducing the human event that gave it meaning.

This distinction does not make AI-generated music worthless.

It does not mean artificial intelligence cannot become a powerful creative partner.

It means we should be intellectually honest about what is being created, who or what is creating it, and what kind of experience is being offered to the audience.

Because if we abandon those distinctions, we risk turning music into an endless stream of technically impressive but culturally disconnected products.

And that would be a remarkable tragedy.

Not because technology defeated humanity.

Because humanity voluntarily surrendered something valuable without even recognizing what it was losing.

One of the old Grendizer doujinshi stories, in which the author created an alternative ending to the original anime. The story begins with the final episode, but takes a very different turn.
In this version, the Duke’s wound never heals. Instead, it continues to threaten his life, leaving him with no hope of recovery. As a result, he feels compelled to confront the Vega Empire alone in space. Before leaving, however, he writes farewell letters to everyone he holds dear, as though preparing for his final journey.
In his letter to Koji, he tells him that he does not have much time left to live and asks him to take care of Maria.
As for Hikaru, he writes her a heartfelt letter expressing his gratitude and appreciation for her kind heart and sincere feelings. He wishes that he had been born on Earth… “Perhaps…” And that is where his letter to Hikaru ends, leaving those unfinished words filled with painful emotions and unanswered questions. 😢
Throughout the story, the artist also illustrates the quiet, intimate moments the Duke and Hikaru shared on Earth, capturing the warmth and closeness they experienced together.
In his letter to Maria, he asks her to stop crying, reassures her that Koji will stand by her side, and tells her that he wants her to be happy. ☹️
Before departing, the Duke remembers the tragic fates of both Naida and Rubina, who left this world never to return. He wonders whether he, too, might meet the same fate.
In the final scene, he boards his spacecraft and heads deep into space to confront Vega. Then, a brilliant flash of light appears in the vastness of space… And that is where the story ends, without the author revealing the Duke’s ultimate fate. Did he sacrifice himself by detonating his spacecraft, or is he still alive somewhere out there? 😢😢😢
As for my personal opinion, I honestly cannot bear such a tragic ending for the Duke and his sister, Maria. I truly wish I could see a happier ending for him, one in which he returns to Earth with his sister, to the home that welcomed them, embraced them, and offered them help and support until the very end.
I don’t like tragic, despairing stories, and I don’t enjoy reading or watching them. 😑😑

text:
Here’s what grok says about them:
Ozark Airlines (Ozark Air Lines) offered a complimentary snack basket that notably included a small bottle of wine, along with typical period snacks.
This was a memorable part of their service on many flights (especially shorter ones in the 1970s–mid-1980s), before the airline was acquired by TWA in 1986. Former passengers and employees have recalled the “snack basket” or related “wine basket” service positively; it stood out for including wine with the snacks rather than just the usual pretzels/peanuts or a basic cookie.
Exact contents varied and are not fully cataloged in surviving public menus or records (Ozark ceased independent operations decades ago, and detailed inflight menus are scarce), but accounts describe a basket with a mini bottle of wine plus assorted snacks typical of regional U.S. airlines of the era—such as pretzels, nuts/peanuts, cookies or crackers, and sometimes cheese, fruit, or similar items. Beverage menus from the period exist in archives (e.g., UNLV Special Collections), but they focus more on drinks than a full snack inventory.
In short, the standout feature remembered by passengers was the small bottle of wine in the snack basket.

text:
🚨 The $25 Million Omar Mystery: Phantom Fortunes, Questionable Citizenship, and Minnesota’s Long Silence

The federal investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar is long overdue, and the latest developments make the red flags impossible to ignore. Agents from Homeland Security Investigations searched her Washington home under a court-approved warrant, seizing phones, computers, notebooks, and her passport. Grand jury subpoenas have gone to family members, including her sister, as prosecutors examine possible false statements and fraud in the family’s immigration paperwork—specifically, whether her age was misstated so she could claim derivative citizenship as a minor when her father naturalized in 2000.

That is not “weaponization.” It is basic enforcement of the law. Citizenship obtained through material misrepresentation is not valid, and Congress has a constitutional duty to ensure its members meet the requirements of Article I. The same standard applies whether the person is a private citizen or a sitting member of the Squad.

The financial disclosures add another layer that demands scrutiny. Omar’s husband, Tim Mynett, saw his reported stakes in Rose Lake Capital and the eStCru winery swing from a few thousand dollars (or less) to valuations as high as $5–25 million in a single year, only for later amendments to dramatically revise those figures downward. Public records show minimal evidence of actual operations, a WeWork-style office, tax problems, an investor lawsuit alleging no legitimate business, and website scrubbing once attention increased. House Oversight has already sought records. When a lawmaker’s household wealth appears to explode overnight while Minnesota has been rocked by massive welfare fraud schemes concentrated in the Somali community, voters and investigators are right to ask hard questions about where the money came from and whether disclosures were accurate.

Minnesota officials, including those who held power while these issues circulated for years, have offered little more than continued political support. Amy Klobuchar was Hennepin County Attorney during the period when Omar’s family navigated the immigration system that is now under renewed review. Tim Walz and Keith Ellison received tips and had executive authority yet took no meaningful action. Ignoring clear anomalies does not make them disappear; it simply shifts the burden onto federal investigators now doing the work state leaders declined to do.

No one is above the law. If the evidence supports charges, denaturalization, or other accountability, it should proceed regardless of political affiliation or the calendar. Equal application of immigration and disclosure rules is not bigotry—it is the minimum standard for a functioning republic. The American people are entitled to know whether their representatives obtained their status and wealth lawfully. That inquiry is exactly what the current investigation is pursuing.

text:
COPPER & AI: The 17-Year Bottleneck — And Two Miners the Market Values Very Differently

$NVDA can deliver GPUs in months. Hyperscalers can build data centers in years. But developing a new copper mine takes 17 years on average.

That mismatch could become one of the defining supply constraints of the AI infrastructure boom.

S&P Global projects global copper demand will rise approximately 50% by 2040, with a potential annual supply gap of roughly 10 million tonnes if additional supply fails to materialize.

But there's a critical distinction investors need to understand:

A genuine copper shortage does not automatically make copper miners attractive investments.

The commodity can be structurally undersupplied while individual mining stocks remain expensive, overleveraged, or unable to deliver their promised production growth.

We examined four producers, then compared two particularly interesting opportunities: Capstone Copper (TSX: CS, OTC: CSCCF) and Hudbay Minerals ($HBM).

One appears to offer more capital-efficient near-term growth. The other controls a potentially transformational U.S. copper development pipeline.

The valuation gap between them deserves attention.

1. First, how much copper does AI actually need?

S&P Global estimates U.S. installed data-center capacity could increase from 62.2 GW in March 2026 to approximately 151.7 GW in 2030.

That's almost 90 GW of additional capacity.

Using an illustrative copper intensity of 35 tonnes per MW, those additions could imply approximately 3.1 million tonnes of cumulative copper requirements associated with data-center facilities.

That is not annual demand, and it should not be added again to an existing global forecast that already accounts for data centers.

The more revealing question is where the copper is needed.

A 2026 study published in Resources Policy estimated that grid transmission and distribution accounted for 64% of copper requirements across its modeled AI data-center infrastructure system.

The precise percentage depends on how infrastructure is defined, but the implication is important.

AI demand doesn't end with GPUs, servers and racks. The electrical system supplying those facilities also requires major investment.

Purchased compute is not the same as productive, energized compute.

And if copper becomes a limiting factor in expanding that electrical system, the economic implications extend far beyond the data-center industry.

2. Capstone Copper: The brownfield growth opportunity

Capstone operates copper assets in Chile, Arizona and Mexico, although it has agreed to sell its Cozamin mine.

For 2026, management guides to 200,000–230,000 tonnes of consolidated copper production and C1 cash costs of $2.45–$2.75 per payable pound.

Its Mantoverde Optimized project is especially interesting.

The expansion has an estimated capital cost of $176 million and is expected to add approximately 20,000 tonnes of annual copper output plus 6,000 ounces of gold on a 100% project basis.

That translates to roughly $8,800 of initial project capital for each tonne of incremental annual copper capacity.

For a capital-intensive industry, that's an attractive starting point.

But there's an important adjustment many investors may overlook.

Capstone owns only 70% of Mantoverde.

Therefore, the incremental 20,000 tonnes represents approximately 14,000 tonnes attributable to Capstone's equity interest.

And there's another complication.

The hidden offset: Cozamin

In September, Capstone agreed to sell Cozamin for total consideration of up to $385 million.

The structure includes $275 million of upfront cash, $15 million of buyer shares, deferred consideration, and copper-price-dependent payments. The full headline amount is not guaranteed cash.

Cozamin's 2026 production guidance was approximately 21,000–24,000 tonnes.

In other words, the attributable copper output added by Mantoverde Optimized alone does not fully replace the production Capstone expects to sell.

That doesn't make the transaction bad.

Capstone is trading an established asset for capital it can redeploy into what management believes are more attractive growth opportunities.

But investors must distinguish gross production growth from net growth attributable to shareholders.

The real question isn't whether Mantoverde expands successfully. It's whether the portfolio produces more sustainable cash flow per share after the sale.

Capstone's longer-term Santo Domingo project offers major additional growth, but its earlier feasibility work estimated initial capital of approximately $2.3 billion in 2023 dollars. Updated capital requirements and financing terms remain important.

Our Capstone thesis: Near-term value creation depends on successfully ramping Mantoverde, improving higher-cost operations, converting the Cozamin sale into balance-sheet strength, and maintaining discipline on future development spending.

The company's growth story is credible, but the capital allocation story matters just as much.

3. Hudbay Minerals: More expensive, but a different proposition

Hudbay is not simply a smaller copper producer.

It currently operates copper and gold assets across Peru and Canada, and its future development pipeline includes two significant Arizona projects: Copper World and Cactus.

Its 2026 copper production guidance is 110,000–138,000 tonnes, substantially below Capstone's consolidated guidance.

However, Hudbay also produces considerable gold.

Gold accounted for approximately 38% of Hudbay's Q2 2026 revenue, and gold by-product credits helped reduce its consolidated reported C1 copper cash costs below zero.

That doesn't mean Hudbay produces copper for free. It means revenues from other metals offset the costs attributed to copper under that accounting measure.

It also means Hudbay is not a pure copper-price bet.

A weaker gold market could change those economics considerably.

Copper World: The major growth catalyst

Hudbay's Copper World project in Arizona is expected to produce approximately 85,000 tonnes of copper annually on average during Phase I, based on its earlier pre-feasibility study.

But Hudbay owns 70%, following Mitsubishi's investment for a 30% joint venture interest.

That implies approximately 59,500 tonnes of attributable annual production, assuming the project achieves its modeled output.

The 2023 pre-feasibility study indicated an initial capital requirement of approximately $1.3 billion before certain financing arrangements, or approximately $1.1 billion after the contemplated precious-metals stream.

Those older estimates imply roughly $13,000 of initial capital per tonne of annual output after the stream.

This is not directly comparable with Capstone's Mantoverde expansion. Copper World involves developing a new mine, its cost estimate is older, and the stream changes the funding economics.

However, Mitsubishi materially reduces Hudbay's burden.

The partnership involves $600 million in committed consideration, with $420 million received at closing and another $180 million due subsequently under the agreement.

Management previously estimated that Hudbay's remaining capital contributions could be approximately $200 million under the pre-feasibility assumptions, with its first contribution deferred until 2028 at the earliest.

That estimate is not a final funding guarantee. Updated feasibility costs, the construction schedule and project economics remain essential.

Hudbay's acquisition of Arizona Sonoran adds the Cactus project, potentially creating a much larger U.S. copper production platform over time.

Management outlines a pathway from approximately 125,000 tonnes of annual copper production toward more than 250,000 tonnes by 2030, with further potential from Cactus afterward.

Those are development ambitions, not completed production.

Our Hudbay thesis: A stronger current balance sheet, meaningful gold-generated cash flow, and a strategically valuable U.S. development portfolio justify paying some premium—but the eventual returns still depend on capital costs, construction execution and production arriving on schedule.

4. The valuation comparison: What are investors paying for?

Using October 15 closing prices:

Capstone Copper
TSX price: C$12.66
Equity market capitalization: approximately US$6.8 billion
Q2 adjusted EBITDA: US$354 million
June 30 reported net debt: approximately US$675 million

Hudbay Minerals
NYSE price: US$24.22
Equity market capitalization: approximately US$10.8 billion
Q2 adjusted EBITDA: US$321 million
June 30 company-defined net cash: approximately US$81 million

Hudbay commands a materially larger equity valuation despite lower current copper output and slightly lower Q2 adjusted EBITDA.

Third-party trailing EV/EBITDA screens show Capstone around 8× versus Hudbay around 10×.

Is the market paying too much for Hudbay's future and too little for Capstone's near-term production?

Possibly. But the simple comparison is not enough to prove mispricing.

Capstone's consolidated EBITDA includes production and earnings associated with noncontrolling interests, particularly Mantoverde. Hudbay benefits from substantial gold exposure and a stronger balance sheet. Both companies also have development projects whose value isn't fully captured by trailing earnings.

Capstone's reported $354 million quarterly EBITDA is not $354 million of distributable shareholder cash. Its 2026 capital budget, including stripping and exploration, totals approximately $790 million.

Hudbay likewise faces significant sustaining and growth spending.

The fair comparison must ultimately be based on attributable, normalized free cash flow and future development capital, not simply consolidated EBITDA or headline copper tonnage.

Still, the valuation gap raises a worthwhile research question.

Which company is offering more for the price?

Capstone wins on nearer-term capital efficiency.

Mantoverde Optimized is already being built around existing infrastructure. Management expects expanded throughput capacity of approximately 45,000 tonnes of ore per day to be sustained beginning in early 2027.

There is less geological and development uncertainty than starting an entirely new mine, although ramp-up, ore grade, labour and operating reliability risks remain.

Hudbay wins on longer-term strategic optionality and current balance-sheet strength.

Copper World has a major strategic partner, important state permits, and substantial potential attributable production. Cactus creates another significant development option.

But investors must pay for the current business and the future projects today, long before all the anticipated output arrives.

The Hayabusa verdict

Our preliminary risk-adjusted research preference is Capstone—but only at the right valuation and with evidence of successful execution.

It offers a nearer-term path to testing the investment thesis. We should know much more about Mantoverde's performance within months rather than waiting several years for a greenfield development.

Hudbay remains a compelling long-duration candidate, especially for investors seeking exposure to potential U.S. copper supply growth.

However, Hudbay's higher valuation makes its future project economics and shareholder returns especially important.

We do not yet see sufficient evidence to declare either stock an outright bargain.

5. What would make us interested in buying?

Here are preliminary valuation watch zones, using the October 15 closing prices as references.

These are alert levels, not calculated intrinsic values or automatic buy recommendations. They provide a margin for further underwriting, assuming the companies' underlying operating outlooks remain intact.

Capstone: C$11.00–11.50 on the TSX

At those prices, we would revisit valuation if Mantoverde demonstrates sustainable throughput improvements, the Cozamin transaction closes as expected, and cash generation supports lower net debt without excessive dilution.

A lower stock price caused by major operational deterioration would not qualify as an attractive entry.

Hudbay: US$20–21 on the NYSE

That would warrant closer examination if Copper World's updated feasibility economics support the financing plan, existing operations remain cash-generative, and the projected U.S. production growth retains an attractive return on invested capital.

Alternatively, unusually strong feasibility results could justify revisiting Hudbay above that range.

Importantly, both companies must be tested under less favorable commodity prices.

A mine that looks cheap at $6.50 copper may look dramatically different at $4.50–$5.00.

We want investments that can survive an imperfect future—not investments that require the most optimistic forecast to come true.

6. The strongest counterargument: The copper shortage could be years away.

This is the part investors should not ignore.

Copper prices have already experienced an enormous rally, and U.S. inventories exceeded 1.6 million tonnes in October, with much of the buildup related to tariff incentives.

Meanwhile, existing mines can expand, previously closed mines can restart, scrap recycling can increase, and expensive copper applications can migrate toward aluminum or other alternatives.

Most importantly, some projected AI data-center capacity may never be energized.

A forecast of 152 GW is not the same as 152 GW of economically productive operating infrastructure.

The world could face a serious copper supply deficit in 2040 while copper equities undergo multiple painful drawdowns between now and then.

For Capstone, our thesis would weaken if Mantoverde fails to sustain expanded throughput, consolidated unit costs remain elevated, or the Cozamin proceeds fail to improve returns per share.

For Hudbay, our thesis would weaken if Copper World's updated capital requirements significantly exceed earlier assumptions, financing becomes more dilutive, or the Arizona production timeline slips materially.

For both, weakening physical copper demand, prolonged inventory accumulation or falling realized copper prices could overwhelm company-specific improvements.

7. The next catalysts

We won't have to wait years for the first answers.

October 29 — Capstone Q3 results: We want evidence on the Mantoverde expansion, throughput, costs, Pinto Valley reliability and balance-sheet progress.

November 12 — Hudbay Q3 results: We'll evaluate free cash flow, copper and gold operating performance, and Copper World financing and development updates.

Late 2026 — Development decisions: Hudbay is targeting a Copper World sanctioning decision; Capstone is advancing Santo Domingo toward its own investment decision.

Those decisions can change future capital requirements and expected shareholder returns materially.

They are more valuable than another round of bullish commodity headlines.

Final Hayabusa Read

We are constructive on copper's long-term structural importance, but cautious about confusing scarcity with immediate investment value.

Capstone is our first-priority valuation candidate because the near-term growth opportunity is more measurable and its valuation screen is less demanding.

Hudbay offers a potentially larger long-duration U.S. copper opportunity, supported by a stronger balance sheet, but investors already pay a premium for that future.

Our posture today: research and watch, not chase. Capstone gets first attention after its upcoming earnings; Hudbay needs updated Copper World economics to justify its premium.

The real investment opportunity isn't necessarily owning the company with the most copper underground.

It's owning the company that can convert copper resources into sustainable cash flow per share, at a cost and entry price the market has underestimated.

That's the distinction between identifying a trend and finding alpha.

Sources: S&P Global, Copper in the Age of AI (January 2026); S&P Global's June 2026 data-center capacity forecast; Amoah et al., Resources Policy (2026); Capstone Copper Q2 2026 results and September 21 Cozamin transaction; Hudbay Minerals Q2 2026 results, Copper World project disclosures, and Arizona Sonoran acquisition; Reuters copper inventory reporting, October 14, 2026. Equity reference prices are October 15, 2026 closing prices. Valuation watch zones are illustrative, not independently appraised fair values.

Disclosure: Hayabusa Research publishes independent research for informational and educational purposes only. Nothing here is investment advice or a recommendation to buy or sell any security.
